displayQuote: The reports of my death have been greatly exaggerated

meta.title: Who really said "The reports of my death have been greatly exaggerated"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Right man, wrong words. Twain's actual note, London, 31 May 1897: 'the report of my death was an exaggeration.' Singular, no 'greatly', and part of a two-sentence explanation about his cousin's illness.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The reports of my death have been greatly exaggerated'?
meta.ogDescription: Twain really did make the remark — but he wrote 'the report of my death was an exaggeration.' The plural and the 'greatly' are later newspaper drift.

answer.label: Genuinely Twain — but not in these words
answer.sourceLine: The remark is real. In London on 31 May 1897, Samuel Clemens handed a written note to a reporter who had been cabled from New York that he was destitute and dying. What he actually wrote was: “The report of my illness grew out of his illness; the report of my death was an exaggeration.” Singular ‘report,’ no ‘greatly,’ and part of an explanation about his cousin — not a standalone epigram.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Handwritten note to a reporter, London

source.excerpt: James Ross Clemens, a cousin of mine, was seriously ill two or three weeks ago in London, but is well now. The report of my illness grew out of his illness; the report of my death was an exaggeration.
trail: A New York paper cabled its London correspondent that Twain was destitute and dying. The correspondent found him alive in London and submitted a written enquiry; Twain replied in writing on 31 May 1897, and the note was printed on 2 June 1897 under the headline ‘Mark Twain Amused’ Quote Investigator ↗.

The confusion was real: his cousin James Ross Clemens had genuinely been seriously ill in London. That is what the note is explaining — the famous clause is the third of three, not an aphorism sourced text ↗.

The drift began within days. A newspaper had ‘greatly exaggerated’ by 3 June 1897; the plural ‘Reports’ appears by November 1897; ‘grossly’ by 1898. Twain himself wrote ‘greatly’ when he retold the episode in 1906, so that word has partial authority — the plural and ‘have been’ never did Wikiquote ↗.
source.excerptNote: The note as printed. Read whole, it is a man patiently correcting a newsroom error about his cousin — the joke is the last six words, and it is drier than the version everyone quotes.
source.rightsNote: Free to reuse. Twain died in 1910 and the note was published in 1897, so both the words and the newspaper text are in the public domain worldwide. You may reproduce it commercially without permission — the only thing to get right is the wording, which almost nobody does. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: About Mark Twain
author.bio: Samuel Langhorne Clemens (1835–1910), writing as Mark Twain, is the most quotable American writer and therefore the most misquoted — the Center for Mark Twain Studies maintains a standing catalogue of things he never said. This is the rarer opposite case: a remark that really is his, worn smooth by 130 years of retelling until the version everyone knows is nobody’s exact words.

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong words
misattribution.intro: The attribution is correct and the source is dated to the day. What has gone wrong is the sentence itself — and unusually, we can watch it change week by week in the newspapers of 1897.

items.why: Twain wrote about one specific report — the false cable from New York. The plural turns a correction of a particular error into a general shrug at the world’s rumours the chain ↗.

The 1897 note has no intensifier. A newspaper added ‘greatly’ within two days and ‘grossly’ followed by 1898. Twain himself used ‘greatly’ when retelling it in 1906 — so that word has some authority; ‘grossly,’ spread by his 1912 biographer, has none.

The line only makes sense as the third clause of an explanation: his cousin James Ross Clemens really had been seriously ill, and a newsroom conflated them. Quoted alone it becomes a witticism about nothing.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Mark Twain, London, 31 May 1897 — but he wrote ‘the report of my death was an exaggeration.’ The plural and ‘have been’ are newspaper drift the note ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is the perfect reply to being written off — unbothered, faintly amused, and delivered by a man who was in fact broke and would spend years on a lecture circuit paying off his creditors. The composure is the joke.

The real note is funnier for being smaller. He is not making a statement about mortality; he is patiently explaining that a newspaper mixed him up with his cousin, and allowing himself exactly six words of dryness at the end.
detailsBody: 31 May 1897, Twain’s note: ‘the report of my death was an exaggeration.’
3 June 1897, a newspaper: ‘reported death has been greatly exaggerated.’
November 1897: the plural arrives — ‘Reports of my death are greatly exaggerated.’
1906, Twain retelling it himself: ‘Say the report is greatly exaggerated.’
1912, his biographer: ‘…the report of my death has been grossly exaggerated’ — the main vector for ‘grossly.’
